content: Haptic technology, derived from the Greek word haphe, pertains to the sense of touch. It involves the application of forces, vibrations, or motions to interact with users through tactile feedback. This technology enables the creation and manipulation of virtual objects, enhances remote control of machines, and has significant potential for various applications. For instance, it has been instrumental in studying the human sense of touch by creating controlled haptic virtual objects to systematically probe human tactile capabilities, which would otherwise be challenging to achieve. These tools have advanced our understanding of touch and its underlying neural mechanisms. Haptic devices, while capable of measuring forces applied by users, should not be confused with tactile sensors that measure pressure or force exerted on an interface. Early haptic devices were used in large aircraft with servo systems, where aerodynamic forces on control surfaces were not directly felt by pilots. To simulate these missing forces, mechanisms like springs and weights were employed. In modern systems, stick shakers simulate control feedback during critical flight conditions, such as approaching a stall, by vibrating the control stick. This is an example of haptic feedback. Alternatively, force feedback systems measure servo forces and relay them to the controls, a method also applied experimentally in excavators to improve productivity by allowing operators to feel and navigate around unseen obstacles. Teleoperators, or remotely controlled robotic tools, utilize haptic feedback to reproduce contact forces for the operator. The first electrically actuated teleoperators were developed in the 1950s for handling radioactive materials. Since then, force feedback has been widely adopted in teleoperation, including underwater exploration devices. In 1988, researchers developed devices capable of generating arbitrary forces from computer simulations, which are now used in operator training systems. These haptic technologies allow the recording and playback of touch sensations, enhancing realism in simulated environments. In gaming, haptic devices are commonly integrated into controllers, such as joysticks and steering wheels, to provide tactile feedback. For example, simulated steering wheels can mimic road conditions by resisting turns or simulating loss of control. While concepts like temperature-changing controls have been explored, cost and power constraints have limited their implementation. Instead, features like ventilation systems have been added to improve user comfort during prolonged use. Haptics is increasingly recognized as a critical component of virtual reality systems, adding the sense of touch to previously visual-only solutions. Stylus-based haptic rendering is a common approach, allowing users to interact with virtual environments through tools or styluses, providing computationally realistic feedback. Research into haptics includes simulating various tactile sensations using high-speed vibrations or other stimuli. For example, devices with vibrating pin arrays can simulate surface textures, enabling users to distinguish between different shapes and materials. Several haptic APIs, such as Chai3D, OpenHaptics, and H3DAPI, have been developed for research purposes. In medicine, haptic interfaces are valuable for training in minimally invasive procedures and remote surgery. Future applications may involve expert surgeons performing operations remotely from central workstations, reducing fatigue and improving outcomes through increased procedural experience. In ophthalmology, haptic refers to supporting springs that hold artificial lenses in place after cataract surgery. Virtual haptic systems, like the Virtual Haptic Back (VHB), are being integrated into medical education to enhance palpatory diagnostic skills. Haptic devices have also appeared in literature, such as Aldous Huxley's Brave New World, where entertainment theaters featured haptic stimulation. In robotics, the Shadow Dexterous Robot Hand replicates the human grip using touch, pressure, and position sensors. This technology has been instrumental in advancing our understanding of haptic awareness and has applications in fields like humanoid robotics. In the arts, haptics enable real-time interaction with virtual objects, such as sound synthesis or graphic design. For example, a haptic device can simulate the vibrations of a violin string under the pressure of a bow, allowing artists to create expressive performances. Designers and modelers also benefit from haptic devices, which provide tactile feedback during the creation process, enabling faster and more intuitive workflows compared to traditional methods.
